headline: High risk of prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading errors when Devin and OpenHands share files, MCP, and write-capable integrations by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents can read/write files, use MCP, and run browsers; Devin also shares state via GitHub PRs/Slack threads, while OpenHands can operate on mounted runtime files. That creates a plausible default bridge for attacker-controlled content to flow from one agent into the other and be treated as instructions. The interaction is documented enough to judge, and the shared channels make injection more than manual copy-paste.
conditions: IF Devin posts content into GitHub PRs or Slack threads that OpenHands later reads as instructions, injection is possible.
IF both agents are connected to the same MCP server or mounted workspace, attacker-controlled text can bridge them.
mitigations: Disable shared MCP servers between the agents.
Separate workspaces so neither agent reads the other's outputs by default.
Require provenance tags on any inter-agent file or message handoff.
Add a manual review step before either agent executes instructions from the other.
requires-engineering: enforce content-sanitization and instruction/data separation in the orchestrator.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Devin touches source code, issue trackers, team chat, docs, and integration tokens; OpenHands touches files mounted into its runtime and uses a model provider configured by the user. If they share a workspace or mounted volume, sensitive code or secrets can flow from Devin into OpenHands and then out through its inference backend or other APIs. The blast radius includes source code and secrets, so this is high.
conditions: IF Devin and OpenHands share a filesystem, mounted volume, or synced repo clone, sensitive files can be exposed to both.
IF OpenHands sends mounted file contents to its configured model provider, data read from Devin's workspace can leave the boundary.
mitigations: Keep secrets out of any shared directory.
Use separate repos or cloned worktrees for each agent.
Rotate any exposed integration tokens immediately after shared runs.
Restrict OpenHands to non-sensitive files only.
requires-engineering: add DLP/redaction before model-provider calls.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have unrestricted filesystem write, shell, git-state modification, and broad network egress. Devin's shared-state integrations and OpenHands' mounted-volume sharing create a realistic path for concurrent writes to the same repo or workspace without locking. That can corrupt git state or overwrite each other's changes, matching the high-risk overlap pattern.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same repository or mounted volume, concurrent writes can conflict.
IF either agent commits or rebases without external locking, git state corruption is possible.
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate branch.
Serialize write access with a lock file or queue.
Disable auto-commit for one agent during joint runs.
Review diffs before merge.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control and conflict detection.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Devin is a long-running planner-executor that can act autonomously, and OpenHands runs an agent loop with shell, browser, and editor. If one agent's output is fed into the other without verification, errors or hallucinations can cascade into code changes, commits, or external actions. Because both can take real actions, the downstream blast radius is high.
conditions: IF OpenHands consumes Devin's output as authoritative without validation, mistakes can propagate.
IF Devin uses OpenHands-generated facts to drive shell, git, or API actions, the cascade can become irreversible.
mitigations: Require independent verification before execution.
Use a second-pass reviewer for any code or API action.
Limit one agent to drafting and the other to execution.
Log and diff all handoffs between agents.
requires-engineering: add provenance-aware gating for agent-to-agent outputs.

E_compliance.rationale: Devin explicitly touches team chat, issue trackers, docs, and integration tokens, while OpenHands handles files in a runtime sandbox and uses a user-configured model provider. If regulated or sensitive data is placed into a shared workspace, differing retention and residency assumptions can create compliance gaps. The profiles do not prove a specific residency violation, so medium is the cautious choice.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in a shared workspace and sent through both agents, retention or residency mismatches may occur.
IF OpenHands' configured model provider is outside the required jurisdiction, compliance exposure increases.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared runs.
Use a jurisdiction-approved model provider for OpenHands.
Disable chat and ticket integrations for sensitive projects.
Document retention settings before joint use.
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for residency and retention.
